promptText: A `let` variable is in the Temporal Dead Zone before its declaration line executes. What happens if you use `typeof` on it in that window, and why does this differ from an undeclared variable?
options: It throws a ReferenceError, because typeof's usual safe-guard for undeclared names doesn't apply to declared-but-uninitialized bindings
It returns "undefined", exactly like an undeclared variable
It returns "undefined", but only in strict mode
It silently returns the value the variable will eventually hold
explanation: typeof normally never throws, even for names that were never declared, but a let/const binding in its TDZ is already declared — just uninitialized — so accessing it (including via typeof) throws a ReferenceError.

promptText: In a React component, `state.items.push(newItem); setState(state.items);` fails to re-render the list. What is the root cause?
options: push() returns undefined, so setState receives undefined
setState(state.items) passes the same array reference, so React's Object.is comparison sees no change and may bail out of re-rendering
push() is asynchronous and hasn't finished by the time setState runs
React ignores array state entirely; only primitive state triggers re-renders
explanation: React detects state changes by reference identity. Mutating the array in place keeps the same reference, so passing it to the setter looks like 'nothing changed' even though the contents differ.

promptText: Why do arrow functions defined as class fields (e.g. `tick = () => { this.seconds++; }`) reliably keep the right `this` when passed as event handlers, while regular methods don't?
options: Arrow functions automatically bind themselves to whatever object calls them
Arrow functions have no `this` binding of their own; they capture `this` lexically from the enclosing scope at definition time, so detaching them doesn't lose it
Arrow functions are hoisted before regular methods, so `this` is already set
Regular methods lose `this` only in TypeScript, not plain JavaScript
explanation: Arrow functions never create their own this binding — they resolve this lexically from where they were defined, so calling them detached (as a bare callback) can't strip the binding the way a regular function's implicit binding can be stripped.

promptText: What is a concrete limitation of the classic `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))` deep-clone trick that `structuredClone()` fixes?
options: JSON.stringify cannot serialize objects at all
The JSON round-trip drops functions and undefined, turns Date into a string, and throws on circular references; structuredClone handles Dates, Maps, Sets, and circular references correctly
structuredClone is faster but has exactly the same feature set
JSON.parse cannot produce nested objects
explanation: The JSON-based hack silently mangles or drops several data types and cannot handle cycles at all, whereas structuredClone is a proper deep-clone algorithm that correctly handles Date, Map, Set, typed arrays, and circular references.

promptText: Why does `const page = input.page ?? 1` behave differently from `const page = input.page || 1` when `input.page` is `0`?
options: They behave identically in all cases
`||` treats 0 as falsy and replaces it with 1, while `??` only replaces null/undefined, so it correctly keeps the legitimate value 0
`??` throws an error when given the number 0
`||` only works with strings, not numbers
explanation: The nullish coalescing operator ?? only falls back when the left side is null or undefined, whereas || falls back for any falsy value — including 0, '', and false — which is a common source of bugs with legitimate zero values.

promptText: Why is `Array.isArray(value)` the correct way to detect an array instead of `typeof value === "array"`?
options: `typeof` on an array literally returns "object", identical to a plain object, so it cannot distinguish arrays at all
`typeof` returns "array" only in older JavaScript engines
Array.isArray is deprecated in favor of typeof
typeof arrays returns "undefined" due to a historical bug
explanation: typeof reports arrays as "object" — the same tag as plain objects, Maps, or null — so it cannot differentiate arrays; Array.isArray specifically checks for the array exotic object internally.

promptText: `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 10); }` logs `3, 3, 3`. Changing `var` to `let` makes it log `0, 1, 2`. Why?
options: let variables are copied by value into setTimeout, while var variables are passed by reference
let creates a fresh binding of i for each loop iteration, so each closure captures its own independent copy; var creates one shared binding for the whole loop
setTimeout only supports let-declared variables correctly due to a spec requirement
var is block-scoped so all callbacks see the final block's value; let is function-scoped so each sees its own
explanation: let is specified to create a brand-new binding per iteration of a for loop, so each closure captures a distinct variable; var has a single function-scoped binding for the entire loop, which is 3 by the time any timeout fires.

promptText: Why might using a plain object as a lookup table for user-supplied string keys be riskier than using a Map?
options: Plain objects cannot store more than a fixed number of keys
A user-supplied key like "__proto__" or "constructor" can collide with inherited properties on a plain object, whereas a Map has no such prototype-chain interference
Objects are always slower than Maps for any number of keys
Map keys must be strings, so this scenario doesn't apply to Map either
explanation: Plain objects inherit from Object.prototype, so a key like "__proto__" can interact with the prototype chain in surprising ways; Map stores entries independently of any prototype, so arbitrary keys (including user input) are safe.

promptText: A dashboard renders five independent widgets, each backed by its own API call. One widget's API is flaky. Which Promise combinator keeps the other four widgets rendering correctly even when one call fails?
options: Promise.all, because it retries failed calls automatically
Promise.race, because it only waits for the fastest call
Promise.allSettled, because it resolves once every promise has settled and reports each one's status individually instead of failing the whole batch
Promise.any, because it resolves as soon as the first widget succeeds and ignores the rest
explanation: Promise.all rejects the whole batch the instant any one promise rejects, which would blank all five widgets; Promise.allSettled always resolves with a per-item fulfilled/rejected status, letting independent failures be handled individually.

promptText: Why is a WeakMap a better choice than a plain Map for caching metadata keyed by DOM nodes that come and go over a long-lived session?
options: WeakMap lookups are always faster than Map lookups

WeakMap holds its keys weakly, so a DOM node no longer referenced elsewhere can still be garbage collected along with its cache entry, avoiding a memory leak; a Map's strong references would keep every node alive forever
WeakMap automatically clears itself every 60 seconds
WeakMap supports string keys while Map does not
explanation: A Map holds strong references to its keys, so caching data keyed by DOM nodes in a Map would keep every node in memory forever, even after removal from the document; WeakMap's weak key references let the garbage collector reclaim both the node and its cache entry.

promptText: In `const a = yield 1;` inside a generator, where does the value assigned to `a` come from?
options: It's always the value that was yielded, i.e. 1
It comes from whatever argument is passed to the next call to `.next(value)`, which resumes the generator and substitutes that value as the result of the paused yield expression
It's always undefined, since yield expressions never resolve to a value
It comes from the generator's return statement
explanation: yield is a two-way channel: the operand of yield is sent out to the caller via next()'s return value, while whatever argument is passed to the subsequent .next(arg) call becomes the value the yield expression itself evaluates to when the generator resumes.

promptText: Why does CommonJS (`require`/`module.exports`) largely defeat a bundler's tree-shaking, while ES Modules support it well?
options: CommonJS modules are always larger in file size than ESM modules

require() is an ordinary runtime function call that can be conditional or computed, so a bundler cannot statically prove which exports are unused without executing the code; ESM's static import/export structure can be analyzed at parse time
Tree-shaking only works with TypeScript, not plain JavaScript
CommonJS does not support named exports at all
explanation: Because require/module.exports are dynamic, runtime operations, a bundler generally can't prove an export is safe to remove without running the code; ESM's imports and exports must be static and top-level, letting a bundler build an exact dependency graph at parse time.

promptText: What is the output order of: `console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("C")); console.log("D");`?
options: A, D, C, B
A, D, B, C
A, B, D, C
A, C, D, B
explanation: Synchronous code (A, D) always runs first; then the entire microtask queue is drained (C, a promise callback) before the event loop even considers the next macrotask (B, the setTimeout callback), regardless of the 0ms delay.

promptText: A developer wraps `const res = await fetch(url); return res.json();` in a try/catch expecting a 404 response to be caught as an error. Why does this silently fail to catch anything, and what mechanism is required to fix it?
options: fetch() only rejects on genuine network failure (DNS error, no connectivity, abort) — it resolves normally for HTTP error statuses like 404, so the try/catch never sees a rejection; you must explicitly check `res.ok` and throw yourself
try/catch cannot catch errors from any async function regardless of what fetch does
fetch() always resolves synchronously, bypassing try/catch entirely
res.json() automatically converts 404 responses into thrown exceptions in modern browsers
explanation: fetch's promise only rejects for network-level failures; an HTTP error status like 404 or 500 is still a 'successful' fetch as far as the promise is concerned, with response.ok set to false — code must check res.ok explicitly and throw to route it into the catch block.

promptText: Inside a Proxy's `get` trap, why is `Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver)` considered safer than simply writing `target[prop]`?
options: Reflect.get is faster because it skips prototype chain lookups entirely
target[prop] throws a TypeError for any object with inherited properties

Reflect.get forwards the receiver argument, ensuring that if the lookup resolves to an inherited getter, that getter's `this` is correctly bound to the original receiver (e.g. the proxy) rather than the raw target — something `target[prop]` cannot replicate correctly through inheritance
target[prop] does not work at all inside a Proxy trap and throws immediately
explanation: When property resolution walks up the prototype chain to an inherited accessor, the fourth 'receiver' argument tells that accessor what `this` should be; Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver) preserves that correctly, while target[prop] always uses target as the implicit receiver, which can be subtly wrong for inherited getters/setters.
